touches.text: Every verb anywhere is reached from the cairn command, as a path: cairn <device> [<machine> ...] <verb>. There is no central list.

help is defined once, as a root verb in the base shim, and answers exactly as `list` does: `help` is the word people type, `list` the system's word. It is readable cold (no bus, no device woken), so `cairn help` answers when nothing else is up. WHY: "help is specifically an anticipation of the behavior of the other monkeys in my species."
`cairn start` (= cairn cairn start) brings the system up: ground loop, bus, shims. `cairn stop` takes it down.
Any cairn command brings up whatever it needs, including the whole install on the very first run (6.3.2). WHY: a well designed tool should disappear in use.

The launcher walks the words. `cairn cairn foo bar` (the long form) means "tell the cairn device to run foo with argument bar". At each level: is the next word a machine here? Step into it and take the next word. Is it a script in this level's bin/? Run it, pass back the result, done. Neither? It is a bus verb: send it to this level over the bus. So `cairn foo bar baz`: foo is a device; it has a machine bar; bar's bin/ has baz, so baz runs. No bar machine? bar goes to foo over the bus. Each check is one directory lookup, so it is fast. WHY scripts first: scripts are the simple path; the bus is the route to what a device answers itself.

Any device or machine may have a bin/ beside its code. That folder IS its list of shortcuts: add a file to add one, delete it to remove one. A shortcut is a script that calls the long form (eg `cairn superclaude` -> `cairn cc superclaude`; `cairn show temp` -> `cairn recovery show temp`), which also saves the walk from searching farther, or does work itself (eg install). Shortcuts live beside what they serve (RULE 1). `cairn foo` whose first word is not a device means `cairn cairn foo`: top-level shortcuts are the cairn device's bin/.

A new shortcut needs no watch. Most instance bins are links to their class bin, so the shortcut is reachable the moment its file lands; the build's proof is the whole guarantee. Akien 2026-11-09, answering Q#75: "why the hell would it need a heartbeat?"

Scripts are Python wherever possible, run by Cairn's own interpreter, so one file works on every platform. Platform-specific ones match their platform: executable or .sh on Linux; .bat, .cmd or .ps1 on Windows.

Repo-root bin/ holds only the launcher itself, the one thing on PATH. Every shortcut lives in the bin/ of the device or machine it belongs to; its bin/ plus its bus verbs is what help lists at that level.
The launcher is Python (bin/cairn), run by Cairn's own interpreter, so Windows needs no bash. Typing `cairn` works on either platform.

In front of it sits a thin platform shell (a shell script on Linux, cairn.cmd or cairn.ps1 on Windows) with enough brains to fall over to Rescue (6.5) when it can't find Cairn's Python, or Python throws, or anything else stops the launcher. The failure throws a trouble ticket (3.4.3), and the ticket is Rescue's "read this" (6.5.3.5); a repeat increments that ticket's counter. Rescue's prompt says: at the end of proving the fix, check for more errors, to clear or fix as appropriate. WHY: trouble has to be able to report when nothing else can (2.3.7.1.3).

Only a failure of the launcher itself falls over to Rescue. A command that runs and fails (eg a verb that exits 1) is that command's error, reported as usual. The Python launcher marks its own failure in a way the shell can tell apart (eg a reserved exit code).
scratch: a proof's throwaway temp dirs and worktrees, cleaned up by the door. WHY: a run must leave nothing behind (4.3.1.7). USERS: the tester.

open_questions.text: The harbor's bus face also answers `clear`: the crossing gate's door (clearance.py), which codemother's `cross` verb already asks, and which CC's cross helper would ask instead of importing clearance (RULE 1, ticket 5e11fadd63b3). You said 2026-10-17 it houses the gates "only because we had to have some place to put them". Is `clear` a harbor verb to add here, or should a crossing reach the gate through another door?
